title: Microsoft responds to LG monitors installing McAfee ads on Windows
gist: LG monitors have been silently installing an app via Windows Update that pushes McAfee pop-up ads with broad system permissions; Microsoft got LG to drop the McAfee ad specifically, but the underlying auto-install loophole and permission scope remain unaddressed, and similar bundling practices have hit other peripheral vendors too.

insights.claim: LG's Monitor App Installer auto-installs itself via Windows Update alongside routine monitor driver updates, then pushes a pop-up ad for a 30-day McAfee trial on affected PCs on every boot, without any prompt or user consent.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Hardware vendors are quietly monetizing driver-update channels with third-party ad placements, a pattern that invites regulatory and reputational risk for both LG and Microsoft.
insights.locator: opening: LG is reportedly pulling a McAfee pop-up ad

insights.claim: The practice is not new: Gamers Nexus editor Steve Burke says he began seeing the pop-up on an LG monitor he purchased three years ago, and Windows Latest noted the installer's changelog recently added McAfee, suggesting the ad-injection has quietly expanded rather than just being newly introduced.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: A years-long, expanding practice signals this is a deliberate monetization strategy rather than an isolated bug, raising the odds of a broader disclosure or regulatory scandal.
insights.locator: As mentioned, some LG monitors appear to have been installing

insights.claim: Microsoft's Windows developer policy allows Universal Windows Platform companion apps tied to a connected device to auto-install without any user notification, as long as the user hasn't opted out of Recommended Settings and is signed into the Microsoft Store — a documented loophole that let LG's installer spread silently.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: The auto-install policy itself, not just LG's app, is the root enabler; investors in Microsoft's platform trust/regulatory standing should watch whether Microsoft tightens this default.
insights.quote: The automatic installation feature does not provide a notification to the user when the app is installed.
insights.locator: Microsoft allows Universal Windows Platform device apps

insights.claim: Once installed, LG's app reportedly has permission to use "all system resources" and to collect geolocation, device data, online activity, contacts, user credentials, and transaction data, according to Gamers Nexus' Steve Burke — a permission scope far broader than what a monitor companion app needs.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Excessive data-access grants on silently-installed hardware software is a live privacy-litigation and regulatory-fine vector (GDPR/state privacy law exposure) for LG.
insights.quote: LG technically possesses permission to use ‘all system resources,’

insights.claim: Microsoft's fix, secured after Gamers Nexus' video went viral, only removes the McAfee pop-up specifically — it does not address the underlying problem of a monitor peripheral silently installing ad-pushing software with broad system permissions onto users' PCs.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: A narrow, PR-driven fix leaves the structural issue (auto-install policy, permission scope) unresolved, so recurrence risk with LG or other vendors remains high.
insights.locator: However, the removal of McAfee doesn’t address the problem

insights.claim: LG is not alone: Razer, Logitech, Asus, and Gigabyte have each previously been criticized for peripherals or components that automatically install unwanted companion software when connected to a PC, indicating this is a systemic hardware-industry pattern rather than an LG-specific incident.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: A sector-wide practice raises the odds of a coordinated regulatory or platform-level (Microsoft) response that could affect multiple hardware vendors' software-bundling revenue simultaneously.
insights.locator: Other hardware vendors have been criticized for their devices

insights.claim: Gamers Nexus paid $1,200 for the LG UltraGear 3GX900A-B monitor used in its testing, only to see its price fall to $600 two days later — a steep, rapid markdown on a premium monitor that also turned out to be silently pushing paid-software ads to its owners.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Volatile discounting alongside undisclosed post-purchase ad monetization suggests LG may be using bundled software revenue to offset margin compression on hardware pricing.
insights.locator: the publication paid $1,200 for an LG UltraGear
